nameStory: The spotfin butterflyfish gets its name from the distinctive dark spot that decorates its dorsal (back) fin, like a bull's-eye target. This eye-catching spot, combined with the fish's flat, disk-like body that resembles a delicate butterfly wing, gives this tropical visitor its memorable name.
description: The spotfin butterflyfish is a stunning tropical visitor that occasionally appears in New England waters during late summer and fall. This disk-shaped fish has a compressed, almost pancake-flat body with bright yellow coloring and distinctive black markings. Adults can reach 6-8 inches in length, making them about the size of a small dinner plate, and they're unmistakable with their elegant, flowing fins and vibrant colors.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark spot on the dorsal fin like a black eye, combined with bright yellow body that feels smooth and slippery to the touch

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened, disk-like body that's taller than it is long, feeling thin as a pancake if handled

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Large, flowing dorsal and anal fins that extend well beyond the body, with delicate rays that feel like soft spines

idTips.label: Head Markings
idTips.description: Dark vertical bar through the eye in juveniles that fades with age, creating a masked appearance

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Reaches 6-8 inches when fully grown, about the size of a small dinner plate

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in shallow coastal waters, often near docks or rocky areas where they seem out of place compared to local fish

habitat: In New England, spotfin butterflyfish are temporary visitors found in shallow coastal waters, particularly around Long Island Sound and southern New England bays. They prefer areas near docks, jetties, and rocky structures where they can find small invertebrates to eat. These tropical refugees are most commonly spotted in protected harbors and warm shallow areas during their brief stay.

seasonality.spring: Absent from New England waters - still in their Caribbean home waters where they spawn and live year-round.
seasonality.summer: Begin arriving in July, carried north by the Gulf Stream as juveniles, appearing in southern New England waters first.
seasonality.fall: Peak viewing time through October when most sightings occur, before water temperatures drop and the fish perish.
seasonality.winter: Gone from New England waters - these tropical fish cannot survive the cold and either die or return south.

funFact: These beautiful fish are essentially oceanic hitchhikers - young butterflyfish get accidentally 'sucked up' by the powerful Gulf Stream current and transported over 1,000 miles north from the Caribbean, like tropical passengers on an underwater conveyor belt they never meant to board!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the four-eyed butterflyfish, but the spotfin has just one prominent spot on the dorsal fin while the four-eyed has distinctive eyespots on its sides. Remember: 'Spotfin = one spot on top, four-eyed = spots on the side.'
contextualKnowledge: These sightings represent 'waif' fish - tropical species carried far outside their normal range by ocean currents. While exciting to see, they're essentially lost and won't survive New England winters, making each sighting a bittersweet glimpse of Caribbean marine life.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative, the four-eyed butterflyfish, the spotfin has its signature spot on the top dorsal fin rather than prominent eyespots on the body sides. The four-eyed also tends to have more complex black and white striping patterns, while the spotfin is primarily yellow with simpler markings. Both species occasionally arrive in New England via the same Gulf Stream transport system.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Spotfin Butterflyfish, the Four-eyed has the distinctive twin eyespots near its tail fin, while the Spotfin lacks these rear eyespots but has a prominent dark spot on its dorsal fin.
